editorial.headline: The Infrastructure Behind Indonesia’s Digital Economy
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 63102 covers the computing, hosting and data infrastructure that keeps digital services available, stored and connected.
editorial.body:
KBLI 63102 is the operating layer beneath a wide range of digital services: the provision of computing infrastructure, hosting and related services that support the management and distribution of data. Its scope includes cloud-computing infrastructure such as Infrastructure as a Service and Platform as a Service, alongside web hosting, streaming-service hosting where content is neither managed nor curated, and application hosting. It is an activity concerned with making digital capacity available—not with the editorial or commercial decisions made through that capacity.

The definition also reaches the less visible but essential machinery of the sector. Shared mainframe facilities may be provided to clients on a time-sharing basis; server and network space can be rented within a data centre through colocation; and electronic data and document storage may be supplied for restricted access, together with other computer-data storage services. What falls outside this activity is customer-requested data processing and data entry. The distinction matters: this is a code for the infrastructure that holds, hosts and enables digital operations.

The activity is open at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. Nationally, it is TERBUKA to foreign investment, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. That makes the national position unusually direct: foreign participation may extend to full ownership within the stated ceiling. The legal source recorded for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali does not reverse that national openness. The province’s standing for this activity is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and it is not blocked by the Bali moratorium. The relevant reason is the risk position at Besar scale: Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, rather than Low or Medium-Low. Bali’s permanent, island-wide PMA restriction applies to Low and Medium-Low risk activities; it does not block this one. For a foreign-owned computing, hosting or data-infrastructure operation, the Bali picture is therefore clear: it can be registered today, subject to the activity’s recorded scope and risk position.
